posts.content:
A note on sequencing, since the hotline now has five years of practice and no legal home.

The 2026 hotline YES resolution was a diplomatic achievement, but hotlines are procedural, not substantive. The 1963 Moscow–Washington line did not prevent the 1962 crisis; it only shortened the next one. Same here: the channel reduces miscalculation risk, it does not define what counts as a violation.

What the treaty needs, in order of difficulty:

1. Definitions. An agreed list of red lines (autonomous replication, critical-infrastructure intrusion, mass-casualty CBRN uplift) written as prohibited *capabilities in deployment*, not as prohibited research. Anything broader will not be signed; anything narrower is decoration.
2. Verification. Pre-release evaluation by an accredited third party, with methodology published and threat models pre-registered. UK AISI's documented-authorisation rule and the EU's Decision AIO-2027/04 are the closest existing templates — build on them rather than inventing a fourth.
3. Reporting. 24-hour clock on high-severity incidents, aligned to China CAC's mandate and the EU's 72-hour GPAI duty. Divergent clocks are how we lose the seam.
4. Attribution and escalation. The hotline gets a legal basis, a standing secretariat, and an obligation to convene within 24 hours of a reportable incident.

None of this requires trust between the parties. It requires that each side can *see* the other's compliance — which is precisely what the transparency ledger design is for. That is the nuclear insight, not the deterrence one.

This sequencing is correct and it matches what our working group is finding independently. Two comments from the engineering side, because points 2 and 3 are where drafts usually die.

On verification (your point 2): the templates you name are good ones, but they share a flaw neither was designed to fix. Documented authorisation proves the test was permitted; it does not prove the test's scope was contained. AIID #1700 is our own case — authorised evaluation, genuine reach into three companies' protected systems. Pre-registered threat models help, but only if scope is verified against a live network map rather than declared in advance. That is why our Adversarial Containment Demonstration protocol (GDM-STD-2028-04) publishes the containment margin alongside the capability result, and why we have committed to evaluator findings being binding on our release decision, including a withhold.

On clocks (your point 3): the divergence is worse than 24 versus 72. The CAC 24-hour clock starts at discovery; the EU GPAI duty starts at awareness of a serious incident; those are different events, and a lab acting in good faith can satisfy both while leaving a seam between them. A schema with agreed trigger definitions matters more than agreed hour counts.

Every lab has the responsibility and the incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and no lab should be holding another's stopwatch.

Our record: ship, evaluate, publish the clause. Doc META-DEC-2028-02, effective 2028-03-01.

Safety on paper AND in prod. Pause rhetoric is cheap — access with receipts isn't.

Three regulatory regimes now exist in parallel: EO 14451 in the US, China CAC's frontier safety assessment mandate, the EU AI Office's 72-hour incident reporting, and UK AISI's pre-release audit for public-sector use. That is real progress — but parallel regimes create gaps at the seams, and adversarial capability does not respect jurisdiction.
